lesson.subtitle: Lesson 26 — Future Plans and Intentions
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 26 — Future Plans and Intentions
lesson.grammar_point: future forms: going to vs will vs present continuous

listenings.text: Here is the test I use before I say anything about the future, and it takes half a second. Is it in the calendar? If somebody else agreed to it and there is a date, I use the present continuous. I am meeting the client on Friday. I am flying on the twelfth. That form means it is arranged, and English speakers hear that immediately. If it is not in the calendar but I have already decided, I use going to. I am going to start the course after the board presentation. Nobody has agreed to that except me, and going to says exactly that. And if I am deciding while I speak, or I am promising something, I use will. Fine, I will send you the notes today. What I try never to do is use will for a plan I made last week. It sounds like I just thought of it, and people plan around what you say. If the form is wrong, the whole calendar in their head is wrong too.

Half of my plans fall through, and I have stopped treating that as a personal failure. What I changed was not the number of plans. It was how I describe them. I used to announce everything with the same confidence, and then quietly let two thirds of it disappear. Now I mark the difference out loud. This is booked. This one I am going to do, but it is not arranged yet. This one I intend to do, and honestly, nothing is set in stone. It sounds like a small thing. It is not. When you say nothing is set in stone, nobody is disappointed if it moves, and they still take the booked ones seriously. That is not pessimism, it is accuracy. And in the long run, being the person whose firm plans are actually firm is worth more than being the person with the most plans.

extra_audio.text: First, I say what is already arranged, with the dates: I am flying on the twelfth. Then I add what I have decided but not booked: I am going to start the course after the review. After that, I mark the soft part honestly: I intend to travel in October, but nothing is set in stone. Next, I say what happens if something falls through, so nobody is surprised later. In the end, I name the one thing that matters most in the long run.

reading.rtitle: My next ninety days — a note to myself
paras: I am writing this down because a plan that only lives in my head never survives a busy week. Three months, three kinds of plan: what is booked, what I have decided, and what is still only an intention.

Booked first. I am flying to Lisbon on the twelfth of October, and I am presenting to the board on the fourth of November. Both are in the calendar, both were agreed with other people, and neither is going to move quietly.

Decided, but not booked. I am going to start the certification course after the board presentation, and I am going to cut my Friday meetings in half. Nobody has agreed to either of these except me, which is exactly why I am writing them here.

And the soft ones. I intend to get around to the reading list I have had since March. We are saving up for a longer trip next year, but the dates are not set in stone. Last year a similar plan fell through in three weeks, and in the long run that taught me something useful: write down which parts are real, and stop pretending the rest are.
